en: *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: Verse Commentary*, Volume One (Zongtong, Scroll 8).
The Eighty Verses of Maitreya Bodhisattva (Versified by Asaṅga Bodhisattva; translated by the Tang Master Yijing).
Verses by Bodhisattva Maitreya, translated by Bodhiruci of the Wei Dynasty;
explained by the Dharma-protector and disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, Nanyue Shan Chang Zeng Fengyi.
(The sequence of the phrases and meanings of this scripture cannot be understood by those in the world who lack clear wisdom.)
The dharma-gates, their meanings, and their sequence— The world does not understand these apart from clear wisdom.
(I bow my head to this teacher who instructs us, Whose body is born of boundless merit.
Great Wisdom thoroughly penetrates and instructs us; I take refuge in the body of immeasurable merit.
(Possessing such virtues as these, one should pay homage; One should bear his footprints upon one’s head.
One should revere him in this manner and more, Bowing the head to his feet and bearing them upon the crown.
The yoke of awakening is difficult to pull, yet he is able to mount it; With resolute mind, he universally benefits all sentient beings.
Because they are able to shoulder the Buddha’s difficult-to-conquer task and because they embrace the welfare of sentient beings, the verse says:
(Supreme benefit should be known; regarding the body and its dependents, attaining what was not yet attained and not falling away from what has been attained—this is called the supreme entrustment).

The meaning of "skillful protection" should be understood as follows: bestowing empowerment upon their bodies and acting in concert with them, so that they do not regress and attain what they have not yet attained—this is called "skillful entrustment.
This explains the two meanings of "skillfully protecting and mindful of all bodhisattvas" and "skillfully entrusting all bodhisattvas.
Protecting and being mindful of them serves to gather in those whose faculties are already mature; the Tathāgata skillfully empowers them through his supernormal powers. Regarding this...

Within their bodies, he causes them to achieve the Buddha-dharma; regarding those who are their companions in practice, he causes them to teach and benefit others, so that in benefiting themselves and others they are no different from the Buddhas.
He entrusts [this task] out of compassion for those whose faculties are not yet mature.
Those who have already attained the stage of non-retrogression, he causes them not to abandon the Mahāyāna;

those who have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression, he causes them to advance further toward the excellence of the Mahāyāna. He entrusts them to one another with this supreme entrustment, desiring that their transformative influence continue without end.
In the mind that is vast, supreme, ultimate, and free from error, where the altruistic intention resides, the merits of this vehicle are fulfilled.
Vast, foremost, and eternal, with a mind free from error, abiding in a profound heart of benefit, the merits of this vehicle are fulfilled.
This explains all categories of sentient beings, up to "those who are not Bodhisattvas," which refers to the four types of mind.
From those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, up to those with neither perception nor non-perception—this encompasses all sentient beings within the three realms.
That they are all included among those to be saved is the vast mind. To cause them all to enter nirvana without remainder.
To bring all beings to the fruition of Buddhahood is the foremost resolve. That in reality there are no sentient beings who attain liberation is because one has extinguished one's own self;
there are no separate sentient beings apart from this. This is the eternal resolve. Why?
Because the Bodhisattva regards all sentient beings as identical to his own body, never abandoning them; therefore, it is called "eternal. If there were a self or a person...
The four marks of sentient beings and a life-span arise from relying upon the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
thus, the notion of "I" and "mine" arises, which is called perversion (*viparyāsa*). To be without these four marks is the non-perverted mind.

Thus, with these four kinds of beneficial intentions, one should practice giving without abiding in anything—the cause for the fulfillment of the fruit. Abiding in non-abiding is called dwelling in the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*).
This vehicle of the Bodhisattvas is perfected in merit and equal in measure to empty space.
Thus subdued and thus established, it is that for which the Tathāgata provides excellent protection and entrustment to all Bodhisattvas.
All six perfections are termed "giving" (*dāna*), categorized as giving material goods, fearlessness, and the Dharma; herein, one, two, and three are called the "practice of non-abiding.
The meaning of generosity (*dāna*) subsumes all six: providing livelihood, fearlessness, and the Dharma; herein, one, two, and three are called the "practice of abiding."

This explanation should carry the meaning of practicing generosity without dwelling on anything. Generosity is the *dāna-pāramitā*, while non-dwelling is the *prajñā-pāramitā*. Why? Because one must be free from signs (*nimitta*) regarding the locus of giving; practicing generosity within the state of being free from signs is called "practice in accordance with reality" (*yoga-caryā*). This is because the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is able to encompass all six perfections. There are three kinds of generosity: [The text continues: ...generosity that is like empty space, generosity that is like an illusion, and generosity that is like a dream. What is generosity that is like empty space? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings, yet perceives neither the gift nor the recipient. What is generosity that is like an illusion? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings, yet perceives neither the gift nor the recipient, and understands that all phenomena are like illusions. What is generosity that is like a dream? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings, yet perceives neither the gift nor the recipient, and understands that all phenomena are like dreams. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is pure, generosity that is impure, and generosity that is both pure and impure. What is pure generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings without seeking reward, fame, or reputation, and does not give out of fear or for the sake of future existence. What is impure generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings seeking reward, fame, or reputation, or giving out of fear or for the sake of future existence. What is generosity that is both pure and impure? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings seeking reward, fame, or reputation, yet also gives without seeking reward, fame, or reputation, and does not give out of fear or for the sake of future existence. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is superior, generosity that is middling, and generosity that is inferior. What is superior generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings with a mind of great compassion, without begrudging even their own body or life. What is middling generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings with a mind of sympathetic joy, without begrudging their possessions. What is inferior generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings with a mind of equanimity, giving only what is necessary. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is internal, generosity that is external, and generosity that is both internal and external. What is internal generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives their own head, eyes, hands, feet, or body to sentient beings. What is external generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives clothing, food, bedding, medicine, or other necessities to sentient beings. What is generosity that is both internal and external? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives both their own body and external objects to sentient beings. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is for one's own benefit, generosity that is for the benefit of others, and generosity that is for the benefit of both. What is generosity for one's own benefit? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings in order to purify their own roots of goodness. What is generosity for the benefit of others? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings in order to bring them happiness and peace. What is generosity for the benefit of both? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings in order to purify their own roots of goodness and simultaneously bring them happiness and peace. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is based on faith, generosity that is based on wisdom, and generosity that is based on both. What is generosity based on faith? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings with deep conviction in the law of cause and effect. What is generosity based on wisdom? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings while understanding that all phenomena are empty and signless. What is generosity based on both? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings with both deep conviction in the law of cause and effect and an understanding that all phenomena are empty and signless. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is accompanied by attachment, generosity that is free from attachment, and generosity that is both accompanied by and free from attachment. What is generosity accompanied by attachment? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings while still harboring thoughts of self, person, being, or soul. What is generosity free from attachment? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings without harboring thoughts of self, person, being, or soul. What is generosity that is both accompanied by and free from attachment? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings while initially harboring thoughts of self, person, being, or soul, yet subsequently realizing that these thoughts are ultimately non-existent. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is mundane, generosity that is supramundane, and generosity that is both mundane and supramundane. What is mundane generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings while still bound by the fetters of desire, form, and formlessness. What is supramundane generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings having transcended the fetters of desire, form, and formlessness. What is generosity that is both mundane and supramundane? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings while partially transcending the fetters of desire, form, and formlessness, yet not having fully transcended them. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is limited, generosity that is immeasurable, and generosity that is both limited and immeasurable. What is limited generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings for only a short period of time. What is immeasurable generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. What is generosity that is both limited and immeasurable? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings for a period of time that is both measurable and immeasurable. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is inferior, generosity that is superior, and generosity that is equal. What is inferior generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings with a mind of stinginess. What is superior generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings with a mind of great compassion. What is equal generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings with a mind of equanimity. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is conditioned, generosity that is unconditioned, and generosity that is both conditioned and unconditioned. What is conditioned generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings while still subject to the conditions of birth and death. What is unconditioned generosity? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings having attained the state of non-arising. What is generosity that is both conditioned and unconditioned? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings while both subject to the conditions of birth and death and abiding in the state of non-arising. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is for the sake of the present life, generosity that is for the sake of future lives, and generosity that is for the sake of both. What is generosity for the sake of the present life? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings in order to obtain wealth, status, or power in this very life. What is generosity for the sake of future lives? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings in order to attain rebirth in the heavens or other favorable realms in the future. What is generosity for the sake of both? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings in order to obtain both worldly benefits and spiritual liberation. Furthermore, there are three kinds of generosity: generosity that is for one's own benefit, generosity that is for the benefit of others, and generosity that is for the benefit of all beings. What is generosity for one's own benefit? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings in order to fulfill their own vows. What is generosity for the benefit of others? It is when a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives gifts to sentient beings in order to relieve their suffering. What is generosity for the benefit of all beings? It is when a
There are three kinds: first, the gift of material sustenance; second, the gift of fearlessness; and third, the gift of the Dharma.

Among these, the gift of material sustenance comprises only the single perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). The gift of fearlessness comprises the two perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*).
The gift of the Dharma comprises the three perfections of diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These are the three kinds of giving.
All of these are termed "generosity," and all are also termed "wisdom. Because wisdom encompasses the five perfections (*pāramitās*), one practices generosity and the others without abiding anywhere.
All bodhisattvas who engage in cultivation should abide in this.
(For the sake of one's own self and for the sake of repaying kindness, one does not cling to any karmic fruit. This is to remain free from non-arising and free from other activities.
One does not cling to the self, nor to repaying kindness, nor to any karmic fruit. To protect oneself is not giving; it is merely guarding against the pursuit of other matters.
This explains the meaning of practicing giving without dwelling on signs (*animitta*). Generally, when people practice giving, it is for only three reasons:
for their own sake in the present, to repay past kindnesses, or in hope of future rewards.
In these three matters of the past, present, and future, one is entirely unattached. What is meant by "not dwelling on things" is that, regarding the necessities of life...
Regarding "generosity" (*dāna*): it refers to having no attachment in the mind toward the material wealth being given. Regarding "non-abiding":

this is spoken in reference to the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*), meaning that when practicing ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*), one does not hope for a reward. Regarding "not abiding in form and so forth": this is spoken in reference to the gift of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*).

This refers to the person who preaches the Dharma, whose mind does not long for agreeable objects, and who remains unattached to all present-life retributions as well as those of future lives. For what reason does he not dwell upon them?
Because his mind is fixed on himself and thus fails to give rise to a mind of generosity; or because, having given, he subsequently regrets it. To guard against such matters, at...
One does not cling to the body. If there is any seeking, one practices giving for the sake of other matters, which leads to the loss of bodhicitta.
To prevent such conduct, one does not cling to things; thus, in acts such as this giving, one should not dwell upon signs.
(They are subsumed within the three wheels; one eliminates conceptualizing regarding signs. Subsequent doubts, as they arise one after another, are all eliminated.
Within that process of taming, one remains far removed from a mind that grasps at signs and severs various kinds of doubt, while also preventing the arising of such a mind.
This explanation shows that merit is obtained through giving while remaining free from signs, and it further severs subsequent doubts.
To save sentient beings while being attached to the four marks is to dwell upon signs even within the act of giving; therefore, this mind that grasps at signs must be subdued.
Thus, within those very acts of giving and so forth, one does not perceive the gift, the recipient, or the giver—within these three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).
One should eliminate the mind that clings to conceptual signs and simply abide as instructed—namely, by abiding in non-abiding. Herein lies a doubt:
if one is free from the conceptual signs of giving and so forth, how can the merit of giving be accomplished?
One does not realize that such giving results in merit that increases further and further, equal in measure to empty space, and beyond all calculation. This is the very point for severing doubt.
Furthermore, as subsequent layers of meaning unfold, all the scriptural passages are intended to eliminate successive doubts. For instance,

when it says, "Do not harbor such thoughts," or "Do not say that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma or saved any sentient beings," these are all meant to prevent the arising of such mental conceptions.

If one were to take [the conditioned] as the collection of formations, the wondrous marks would not be the supreme marks, because the three characteristics are subject to change and difference. Since there is no such thing [as a permanent self], this is called the Tathāgata.
To analyze the nature of the conditioned is to prevent the attainment of that [false] accomplishment; because the three characteristics differ from its essence, being free from them is the Tathāgata.
This explanation clarifies the meaning that the Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of physical characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata are produced through the accumulation of causes and conditions such as generosity; they fall within the category of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and are achieved only after practicing for many eons.
If one were to discriminate and regard the essence of the conditioned as the Tathāgata, then one would perceive the Tathāgata as something conditioned.
Regarding its superior characteristics: if one considers the Tathāgata’s nature of *tathatā*, such superior characteristics do not exist. Why is this?

Because this conditioned entity is subject to being transformed by the four characteristics of arising, abiding, change, and cessation. As for the statement that these three characteristics are distinct entities, it is because abiding and change occur simultaneously.
If one refers to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, he is fundamentally unarisen and free from [these characteristics].
That which is conditioned is fundamentally without anything to be done. It is apart from accomplishment; it is not born in the past limit, nor does it perish in the future limit.
It is fundamentally without change and is apart from distinct entities, because the three marks are different from the Tathāgata. This is the Dharma-body, which is signless;
one should not perceive it through physical characteristics. If, in this regard, the three marks cannot be apprehended, it is sufficient to know [this].
The Tathāgata is not something produced by the causes and conditions of conditioned activity.
Having seen this, although one practices giving for the sake of the fruit of Buddhahood, one does not become attached to the gift of Dharma; thus, by accomplishing such a severance of doubt.
The profound meaning of cause and effect was taught during that degenerate age; it is not without benefit, for it is endowed with the three qualities of a bodhisattva.
The profound significance of cause and effect was proclaimed in that evil world; it is not in vain, as it possesses reality, being fully equipped with the three virtues of a bodhisattva.
"Because he upheld the training in the precepts under previous Buddhas and planted roots of goodness, he is said to be 'endowed with precepts' and 'endowed with virtue.
Having cultivated the precepts in the past and planted various roots of goodness, he is endowed with the precepts of all Buddhas; thus it is also said that his virtues are fulfilled."
This explanation pertains to the meaning of how there are sentient beings who plant various roots of goodness. "Abiding in non-abiding" refers to the profundity of the cause;
"having marks yet being markless" refers to the profundity of the fruit.

In this era of strife, contention, and entrenched evil, those who are able to avoid treating this as mere empty talk and instead give rise to true faith are the bodhisattvas of the final age who uphold the precepts.
They cultivate merit and are fully endowed with precepts, virtue, and wisdom; because these three qualities are complete, they are able to have faith.
One should know that such persons cultivated the precepts in the past, served many Buddhas, and planted various roots of goodness long ago.
There are three meanings to making offerings to the Buddhas: first, attending to them at their side; second, preparing all that is required.
Third, because one can guard the essential points of the Dharma through inquiry and reception, it is called *śīla*. This means being able to skillfully guard the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of cultivation: first, the ability to distance oneself from the ten unwholesome actions;

second, the ability to perform the practices conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣika-dharma*); and third, the ability to proceed toward the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Such is its cultivation.
By practicing respectful service while observing the precepts, one is fully endowed with morality (*śīla*).
By making such offerings and planting roots of goodness, one is fully endowed with merit (*puṇya*). Next, the following clarifies their endowment with wisdom (*prajñā*):
being able to give rise to the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) within Bodhi, their merit becomes perfect; thus, their blessings are truly immeasurable.
Because one can sever the notion of a self and the notion of phenomena, this is called being endowed with wisdom. (The two sets of four become eight).
That person and those phenomena are far removed from grasping at signs; yet it is also said that one knows those signs. This is based on the distinctions among the eightfold and eightfold meanings.
(A separate entity arises in succession; it persists until the end of one’s lifespan, then seeks another realm of existence. There are four kinds of the notion of self).
The entity that continues in a distinct succession, remaining uninterrupted until life ends, and then proceeding toward a different path—these are the four kinds of the characteristic of "self."

(All are non-existent because they lack intrinsic nature; they exist because they cannot be described [as having such a nature], for they are the basis for verbal expression. There are four kinds of conceptualizations regarding phenomena.
All things are empty and without substance; their actual existence cannot be described. They are spoken of by relying on words and phrases; these are the four kinds of characteristics of phenomena.
This explains the four marks—the self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span—and the meaning of neither the mark of phenomena nor the mark of non-phenomena.
It was stated above that the Bodhisattva is endowed with the three virtues: from precept arises concentration, and from concentration arises wisdom.

That which is called "possessing wisdom" refers to one who thoroughly understands the selflessness of persons; therefore, they are free from the four marks including the life-span. They also thoroughly understand phenomena...
Because there is no self, there are no four characteristics of either phenomena or non-phenomena. That life-principle (*jīva*) and its phenomena are both devoid of the eight characteristics;
one no longer grasps or clings to them. Who is it that knows those characteristics and distances themselves from them? Only the one endowed with wisdom.

Relying upon the eight characteristics, they thoroughly understand the distinct meanings of the eight characteristics. What are the four kinds of the characteristic of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*)? Within them, there is a sovereign controller.

That which is designated as "self" is now observed to consist of the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Each of these is distinct and individually lacks a sovereign master;
therefore, there is no characteristic of a self. That which abides in a permanent nature is called a "sentient being. Now, these aggregates are impermanent.
It flows on in continuous succession; there is not a single dharma that possesses a nature of abiding. Therefore, there is no characteristic of a sentient being (*sattva*).

This uninterrupted continuity from moment to moment is called the "abiding of life. Now, it abides until the exhaustion of its lifespan. As a sutra says: "In this very moment, you are born, you age, and you die.
Therefore, there is no characteristic of a life-span possessor (*jīvaka*). The aggregates (*skandhas*) circulate in rotation, undergoing various transformations.
The "destinies" (gati) are called the "personality mark" (pudgalanimitta). Within these, there is no person who can grasp the destinies.

It is like an image appearing because of a physical object; the object does not reach the image, yet the image appears. Because of the preceding aggregates (skandha), the subsequent aggregates arise in succession;

the preceding does not reach the succeeding, yet they continue in a stream. This is what is meant by the absence of a personality mark. This is called the realization of the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya).
This is the nature [of reality]. What are the so-called four kinds of dharmic characteristics? A sutra states: "There is no perception of dharmas, nor is there perception of non-dharmas;
there is no perception, nor is there non-perception. This is the case in all translations, though the Qin version omits the latter two. Why is this so?
Because in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), dharmas are fundamentally unarisen; the grasper and the grasped—indeed, all dharmas—are entirely non-existent. Therefore...
There is no perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), because they do not arise; nor is there cessation. Those phenomena are without substance, yet emptiness truly exists.
Therefore, there is also no perception of non-phenomena (*adharmasaṃjñā*). This verse refers to the fact that all things are empty and without substance.

Because phenomena and non-phenomena are free from conceptual differentiation, they cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said to be non-existent; for they are not what can be expressed by words. Thus...
"Non-conceptualization. This verse refers to that which truly exists yet is inexpressible. What is called "non-conceptualization" merely reveals the absence of conceptualization;
it does not mean that there is a dharma named "non-conceptualization. Although the ultimate truth transcends all conceptualization, it is described by means of worldly linguistic concepts.
For one speaks of the ineffable by relying on the characteristics of language; thus, it is inexpressible.
The "manifest" is the cause for actual verbal expression; furthermore, there is no "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This verse refers to speaking in reliance upon words and phrases.

This is called the thorough knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). The four characteristics such as "life-force" (*āyus*) are easy to understand, whereas the four characteristics such as "phenomena" (*dharma*) are difficult to discern.
When one knows that these are devoid of the four characteristics of self, person, sentient being, and life-force, this is what is meant.

The characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), together with those very characteristics, are themselves empty; this is what is called "non-characteristics. To have "is" and "is not" is still to remain within conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
When both "phenomenon" and "non-phenomenon" are extinguished, there is nothing that can be expressed; this is called "universal emptiness" (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*).

If one were to maintain that all is exclusively empty, thereby destroying all characteristics, one fears falling into a biased emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā*); therefore, one relies upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
It is taught that there is neither the mark of existence nor the mark of non-existence. It exists yet does not exist; it is non-existent yet is not non-existent.

This is the Truth of the Middle Way. Here, "not dharma" (an-dharma) negates the mark of dharma; "markless" (animitta) negates [the mark]; and "neither the mark of non-existence" negates the negation of the negation.
The Qin translation merely subsumes this under the characteristic of non-dharma (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*).

(This is because, through the power of their faith and understanding—due to faith, they give rise to the notion of reality; yet, because they do not grasp according to the literal expression, they take it as the correct teaching.)

That person, relying on faith and generating a sense of reverence, gives rise to the perception of reality. Upon hearing sounds, they do not grasp them erroneously; rather, they grasp what is correctly taught.
This explains that one should not grasp at dharmas, nor grasp at the meaning of non-dharmas. That person maintains the precepts and cultivates merit.
One is able to give rise to deep faith. Relying upon that faith, one reveres many Buddhas, plants various roots of goodness, and hears this sutra.
Even if one gives rise to pure faith for but a single thought-moment, that faith becomes purified and is able to produce the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Because those endowed with wisdom do not grasp the meaning according to the literal expression, but rather accord with the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and take it as the correct teaching, it is called [the "True Dharma"].
This is for the sake of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). For this reason, after explaining that those eight marks are to be relinquished, it is said:
"One does not grasp at the mark of dharmas, nor does one grasp at the mark of non-dharmas. Both dharma and non-dharma have not yet transcended verbal teaching (*śabda-śāsana*);
however, one does not correctly grasp them by means of the verbal teachings one has heard. One does not correctly grasp dharma... [text ends]
To correctly grasp what is non-dharma is to be free from the two marks; this is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

To speak of it as being grasped in this way is, therefore, to grasp by means of non-grasping. When those bodhisattvas hear these spoken phrases, they are able to give rise to the true mark in this manner.
Why worry that those who hear of this later will not develop genuine faith?
(The Buddha’s realization of the fruit is incomparable; it is known through his vow-knowledge [praṇidhijñāna]. This is to prevent those who seek profit and honor from making such claims themselves.)
The Buddha does not know by means of perceiving results; rather, his power of wisdom (*jñānabala*) perceives them directly. When others seek offerings and honor, they are unable to explain this.
This explains the meaning of the Tathāgata’s “knowing all and seeing all”: for the Buddha, knowing is itself seeing, and seeing is itself knowing.
It is not like the fleshly eye, which sees only coarse and proximate objects, yet fails to know what is extremely subtle, obstructed, or distant.
This is not like inferential knowledge (*anumāna*), which perceives fire by seeing smoke; such knowledge cannot illuminate the distinctions between various characteristics.

The Buddha knows each and every fruition of those who possess the precepts and other virtues; the Buddha sees each and every one of them. If he did not say "sees," one might think it is known through inference;
if he did not say "knows," one might think it is seen with the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) and so forth. Therefore, both "knowledge" and "vision" are mentioned together.
Nevertheless, this is understood through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*).

Because only the Buddha possesses the great power of the vow to extensively deliver sentient beings, and because he possesses the great power of wisdom—the knowledge of all modes of knowledge—he clearly awakens to all objective spheres.

Not only does he illuminate the fruits of merit in the present life without error, but he also perceives the retributive results to be experienced in the future, such that people shall offer him worship.
Regarding the immeasurable merit of reverence and so forth, [the Buddha] understands each and every one of them. Why did the Tathāgata speak in this way?
Those who possess the precepts and so forth and wish to obtain merit would not be able to explain it themselves; for such a person knows it by their own realization.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, thoroughly know what kind of person that is and what kind of conduct they possess; therefore, that person cannot speak of it themselves.

There are two kinds of merit: that which is "produced," because it is the cause capable of producing [the result]; and that which is "appropriated," because it has the sense of being the fruit that perfumes and cultivates one's own continuum.
(One realizes non-abiding in phenomena; because this is a matter of conformity, it should be understood as having an intentional meaning, like abandoning a raft.
That non-abiding conformity is the realized wisdom regarding phenomena; it is like a person abandoning a boat or raft—the principle regarding phenomena is likewise so.
Even this teaching of the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone that which is not the Dharma.

This refers to the teachings of the *prajñāpāramitā* of words, such as the *sūtras*, because they are not the dwelling place of those who have attained realization. Once realization has been attained, one should relinquish those teachings.
Just as one who has reached the other shore should abandon their raft, so too, while desiring to realize wisdom, it is not that the Dharma may not be relied upon;

because it is conducive to the higher realization, it must be gathered. Just as one who has not yet reached the shore must certainly rely upon the raft, this is called the "intentional meaning" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
Since there is both taking up and discarding regarding a single raft, it is termed "intentional. This is the Dharma of Prajñā. Regarding...
Even that which corresponds to signless bodhi is still something to be relinquished; how much more so the four kinds of self-characteristics and the four kinds of dharma-characteristics?
How could one who does not correspond with the true nature (dharmatā) take up attachment and fail to relinquish it?
That which follows after dharmas without awakening is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which awakens and is able to transform dharmas is called [wisdom].
Wisdom: the transformation of consciousness into wisdom is precisely the meaning within the Dharma.

(The manifested body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma; the preaching of the Dharma is free from the duality of grasping, and that which is preached transcends all verbal expression.)

The manifested transformation body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma. When preaching the Dharma, one does not grasp at duality; there is no preaching, as it is free from the marks of words.
This explains that all teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are neither graspable nor expressible; this is the meaning of being neither a phenomenon (*dharma*) nor a non-phenomenon (*adharma*).
This is the meaning of the Tathāgata having neither attainment nor preaching, as understood by Subhūti. The manifested transformation body is not a [substantial] phenomenon.
The body originally does not realize the Dharma, nor does it preach the Dharma; therefore, it is said that there is no fixed Dharma to be attained, nor any fixed Dharma to be preached.
What is the meaning of this? It is because the True Suchness (tathatā) taught by the Tathāgata cannot be heard by the ear, for it is ungraspable;
it cannot be proclaimed by the mouth, for it is ineffable. Therefore, one should know that it is not a dharma.
It is neither non-dharma; this is spoken according to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness). It is not dharma, because its nature is that of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Yet it is also not non-dharma, because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) while its essence exists.

Being free from both extremes, it is ineffable; it is unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*), which transcends the characteristics of verbal expression and has never existed [as such] from the beginning.

As for "attainment," since there is nothing to be attained, what more is there to say? This state of non-attainment and non-explanation is why Subhūti is foremost among those who understand emptiness.
(Receiving for oneself and teaching others is not without benefit; it is the accumulation of merit. Merit alone does not sustain enlightenment, for those two together can sustain it.
Receiving, upholding, and teaching the Dharma are not fruitless in terms of merit. Merit alone does not lead to enlightenment; these two can lead to enlightenment.

Because it is the cause for attaining intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-hetu*), that which remains here is "arising" (*jāti*); since these are exclusively the qualities of the Buddha, they can accomplish the most supreme merit.

Regarding the real name, it is the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*), and it also serves as the cause for the arising of the others; being solely the qualities of the Buddhas, merit is established as the primary essence.

This explanation means that even if one were to fill the three-thousandfold world system with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, that which is called "Buddha-dharma" is, in its true sense, not Buddha-dharma.
[The text continues: "Filling the three-thousandfold world system with treasures and holding them forth to give as a gift."
It is not that they do not obtain vast merit; however, because they do not incline toward Bodhi, they merely accomplish tainted (*sāsrava*) karma.
If one upholds this sutra and explains it for others, then through both self-benefit and benefiting others, one can incline toward Bodhi and shoulder the path of the Buddha.
The accumulation of such merit far exceeds that of the aforementioned gift of jewels, being immeasurably superior. How could one even speak of it otherwise?
This is the excellence of merit. All unsurpassed bodhi is revealed through this sutra.

One realizes the unconditioned reality-body (*asamskṛta-dharmakāya*) here and now and forever severs the causes of birth-and-death suffering; therefore, it is said that [this sutra] serves as the "causal condition for realization" regarding reality.

All Buddhas have perfumed and cultivated their body and speech through this sutra, thereby perfecting their ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) and giving rise to the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*.
Therefore, it is said that this also serves as the cause for future births. Those who uphold and expound this sutra achieve the foremost Dharma;
they achieve the rare Buddha, the merit of the world—what could surpass this?
Yet, what is called the Buddha-Dharma is neither Buddha-Dharma nor non-Buddha-Dharma, because the Dharma realized can only be personally realized by a Buddha. The Buddha...
It does not belong to oneself because it is not shared with others. Since it can serve as the primary causal condition for all phenomena, this merit is the most excellent among all forms of merit;
therefore, it is said that this merit constitutes the supreme essence.
Because one does not grasp at its own fruit, it is neither graspable nor expressible; because it liberates one from the two obstacles, Subhūti is said to be "without contention.
It is ungraspable and inexpressible because its own fruit is not grasped; based on that, the Well-Gone One taught the departure from the two kinds of obstacles.
This explains whether a *srotāpanna* can think, "I have attained the fruit of *srotāpatti*.
As for Subhūti, he truly has nothing to practice, yet he is named Subhūti; this is the meaning of delighting in the practice of *araṇā*.
All noble sages are distinguished by means of the *asaṃskṛta-dharma* (unconditioned dharma). What is called the Buddha-dharma today is...
This is not the Buddha-dharma; it is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), which is likewise neither to be grasped nor to be spoken of.

What is called "not to be grasped" does not mean that its fruit does not exist. For example, those who have attained the four fruits each realize their own respective fruit, yet they do not form the thought, "I have attained this fruit.
This is what is meant by non-grasping. At the time of realization, they are free from grasping at a self (*ātman*) and so forth.
Because of the affliction of sleep, there is no such mind as "I can attain the fruit.

This non-appropriation is precisely the four fruits being free from the four fruits, just as it was taught by Subhūti regarding the attainment of the *araṇā-samādhi*. As for "non-contention" (*araṇā*):

This means being free from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and being free from the obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhivaraṇa*). By being free from the obstacle of afflictions, one attains the fruit of Arhatship;

by being free from the obstacle to meditative concentration, one attains the practice of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*). Since both persons and phenomena are empty, what further could there be to grasp?

(At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he spoke of not grasping at the realization of dharmas; it is by means of this that the realization of dharmas is accomplished, for it is neither something grasped nor something spoken.
Regarding the words of Dīpaṃkara, the Buddha did not grasp at the wisdom of ultimate reality; by virtue of this true meaning, that teaching of non-grasping was established.
This explains the meaning that when the Tathāgata was in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he actually attained nothing regarding the Dharma.
When Dīpaṃkara was born, the radiance of his body was like a lamp; because this continued until he attained Buddhahood, he was also named Dīpaṃkara.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata received the prediction of future Buddhahood from him. However, within the words of Dīpaṃkara’s prediction, the Buddha did not grasp at any dharma. There is none.

The perception of a Buddha, the perception of a self, and the perception of receiving a prediction of enlightenment when no prediction has been given—these are shown to be the realization of wisdom, for there is nothing to be grasped.
Rather, by means of non-conceptual, ultimate wisdom, one realizes the undifferentiated true reality.

By virtue of this meaning of truth, one is free from the marks of mental objects and thus achieves non-grasping; one is free from the marks of verbal expression and thus achieves non-explanation. Regarding that which is...
Because when the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly attained nothing regarding the Dharma.
(The flow of wisdom is the nature of consciousness-only; the land is not an object of grasping. Because it is formless and supreme, it is not adorned, yet its nature is that of being adorned.)

Through the mastery of the consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra) practice by means of wisdom, one thus grasps the pure land. It is not a physical form; it is the primary essence. It is not an ornamentation; it is the intention of adornment.
This explains that what is called "adorned Buddha-land" is in fact non-adornment, which is the meaning of "adornment.

There are two kinds of pure lands: first, the land of dharmalakṣaṇa (phenomenal characteristics), which possesses perceivable forms and marks; second, the land of dharmatā (the nature of phenomena), which is free from [such marks].
All marks are beyond seeing or hearing. There are also two kinds of adornment: first, the adornment of form, which refers to the golden ground, jewel-pools, and so forth;

second, the adornment of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which refers to the cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the penetration of the true principle of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
By manifesting merits that exceed the sands of the Ganges, these serve as adornments, as follows:
Thus one takes up the Pure Land. This is not a Pure Land of form; rather, it is the Pure Land of the primary essence (*prathama-tattva*).

Such adornment does not consist in taking up signs as adornment; this is true adornment. According to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no substantial form to be grasped, and thus it is not adornment.
According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), such [adornment] is non-adornment.

"Adornment. This is what is meant by "adornment. If one clings to the idea that there are superior forms and adornments in Buddha-lands and thinks, "I shall achieve them," then one possesses a mind of attachment toward objects such as form. To prevent this view, it is followed below by the instruction:
"One should generate the mind by dwelling nowhere."
Just as Mount Sumeru is without grasping in its enjoyment, because it is not of a nature characterized by outflows (*āsrava*), nor is it produced by causes;
so too is the experience of retribution without grasping, for it is far removed from all outflows and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

This explains the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching that what is not a body is called a "great body. Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is like the king of Mount Sumeru:
although Mount Sumeru is vast, it does not conceive the thought, "I am the king of mountains," because the mountain lacks a discriminating nature.
The reward-Buddha is likewise; he does not conceive the thought, "I am the Dharma-king," because he is free from discrimination. How could this be...?
Is this non-conceptual? Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), both mountains and the physical body (*rūpakāya*) lack any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

therefore, the Buddha taught that it is "no-body," which is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*). Because the Buddha who receives the retribution of bliss is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*), he is without any substantial entity;
thus, he is "no-body. It is because of this absence of a [substantial] body that he is said to possess a body—there is only the pure body.

Therefore, its own essence exists inherently and is not produced by causes; because it is far removed from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), it is the "Great Body," which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
(In order to manifest its many distinctions and its attainment of excellence, and because the merits [of the preceding and succeeding stages] differ, further similes are set forth.)
This explains the distinctions among many meanings and establishes a superior comparison; the subsequent merit exceeds the former, and therefore a further superior analogy is stated.
This interpretation—that it is "like the number of grains of sand in the Ganges River"—refers to the meaning of surpassing the aforementioned merit. One might ask:
"Since the analogy of the gift of jewels was already explained previously, is this not a redundancy? The previous statement referred to a single trichiliocosm.
Regarding the "gift of jewels": this refers to the gift of jewels filling immeasurable trichiliocosms.

Although both [the previous and current gifts] are extensive in scope and involve superior comparisons, the latter is the most extensive among the extensive and the most superior among the superior; therefore, it is stated again.
Why does the subsequent merit exceed the former? It is because the cause for establishing the distinctions of the former merit was not clearly explained.
Since [the previous examples] lack the capacity to sustain the realization of bodhi, I now wish to manifest the characteristics of the causal factors that can establish it.
Therefore, I shall employ further distinct analogies to explain this according to specific matters; thus, the analogy of weighing and measuring is likewise preeminent.

(Because both are equally respected; because of the excellence of their outflow; because they are the causal nature of afflictions; and because they are both inferior and superior). Respect is due in two respects:
as the cause for cultivation and realization of the Great Essence (*mahātman*), and as the cause for the cultivation of afflictions. This [merit] subdues defilement and brings forth merit.
This commentary explains the passage from "whosoever shall preach even so much as a single four-line verse of this sutra" up to "this is called the meaning of the thirty-two marks.
Regarding the two locations: one is the place where a four-line verse or the like is preached; the other is the location where the scripture itself resides.
At the place where a four-line verse is preached, all devas and humans should offer worship as if it were a stupa of the Buddha.
A temple is already held in high esteem; however, a place where the scriptures are located is even more supremely revered, as if a Buddha or a disciple of the Buddha were present there.
Even when one gives gifts of the seven treasures and the like, neither the site where the jewels are given nor the donor possesses such a quality.
Therefore, it is said that upholding and expounding [this scripture] is superior. Furthermore, the name of this sutra is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

Honey is *prajñā* itself, yet it is distinct from *prajñā*. This is because it serves as the supreme cause for all Buddhas and Tathāgatas to realize the Dharma, and because it is that which all Buddhas collectively proclaim; thus, they all take the cultivation of *prajñā* as their cause.
Realizing the nature of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and illuminating the Great Matter (*mahā-vastu*), there is nothing that can be said, yet it is said;

therefore, it is called "realizing the Great Essence through practice. The merit of giving those seven treasures is a cause for defiled afflictions (*kleśa*), because it can bring about the affairs of affliction—just as the accumulation of minute particles forms a world—and thus does not transcend the causes and effects of humans and devas. This is...
Since both cause and effect are not substantially real, it is said that they are neither atoms nor worlds.

Yet, these "atoms" are not the essence of afflictions such as greed, and this "world" is not a realm that serves as the cause for the defilement of afflictions; therefore, they are called "atom-worlds.
These worldly dusts are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); they are not reached by those defiled afflictions. Even if one were to obtain merit from them, it would be like [an atom]...
Even things such as the worlds of dust are likewise indeterminate (avyākṛta) and extremely inferior;
how much more so is this merit of upholding the sutra, which can distance one from the causes of affliction, bring about the Bodhi of a Buddha, and achieve the thirty-two marks?
Is this not the most supreme merit among all merits? Furthermore, the thirty-two marks are not the essential nature of perfect enlightenment;

therefore, they are merely called the "thirty-two marks. Compared to the ability to attain the nature of great enlightenment through upholding and expounding this Dharma-gate, [the marks are inferior].
These [marks] may also be considered inferior. Although these physical marks of the Buddha are inferior, they are nonetheless supramundane merit;
they truly surpass the defiled worldly merit obtained from giving jewels.
How much more so the cause of the Dharma-body, which not only transcends these thirty-two marks but can also subdue defiled merit—indeed, the merit of upholding this sutra can further subdue it.
(Because its fruit is superior to suffering; because it is a sublime matter difficult to encounter; because the shore of its object is unknowable; and because it is unique among others.
The body of suffering is superior to that [other world]; it possesses the sense of rarity and supremacy. The shore of that wisdom is difficult to measure, and it is not the same as other dharmas.
Because its nature is profound, because it excels other abbreviated expositions, because its lineage is noble and superior, and because it surpasses merit among merits like a jewel of fortune;
it possesses a firm understanding of the profound meaning, excelling other sūtras through its great causes and purity—it is the supreme merit among all merits.
This commentary explains that the meaning of the first *pāramitā* consists in giving away one's body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

When one gives away immeasurable bodies and lives in this manner, compared to the merit and the fruit of reward obtained by those who give material wealth and possessions, this merit surpasses theirs. Why is this? Because they [the former] sacrifice their bodies and lives.

Because it afflicts both body and mind, it is a cause of suffering that ultimately brings about the fruit of suffering. If one were to give even a single four-line verse as a gift, one would be liberated from the ocean of suffering;
would not such merit be far more excellent? At that time, Subhūti, out of reverence for the Dharma, shed tears. "This Dharma-gate is rare;
though one possesses the eye of wisdom, one has never heard it before. Furthermore, it is difficult [to encounter]."
Furthermore, this is a superior matter. Why is it superior? Because of the aforementioned meaning. As the Sūtra says:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is not [merely] the Prajñāpāramitā. That shore of wisdom cannot be measured by anyone; how, then, could one reach it?
It is because the shore of the object known belongs solely to the Buddha, and no one else is able to know it. Therefore, it is called the "superior meaning. Moreover—
This Dharma-gate is unlike other teachings because within it there is the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Apart from the Buddha-dharma, no other place possesses this true mark;
therefore, when the mind of faith is purified and one does not believe in other teachings, the true mark arises. As for what is called the "true mark":
It exists only here. To say it is not real means that it does not arise elsewhere; yet this sign is capable of arising and shall bring about the accomplishment of the most rare and marvelous merit.

Furthermore, because this dharma-gate is of a profound nature, those who are able to receive and uphold this sutra, contemplate and practice it, and do not give rise to the notion of "self" and so forth, are [engaged] with respect to the objective sphere of what can be grasped.
There is no perversion; one attains the selflessness of persons. Furthermore, the marks of "self" and "mine" are themselves non-marks;
this is the grasping at a self, yet there is no perversion therein, and thus one attains the selflessness of phenomena.

These two, in their respective order, clarify the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena, culminating in the emptiness of emptiness itself. Being able to depart from all marks is what is called being a Buddha; therefore it is said:
This is the meaning that is true, firm, and profoundly deep. The Buddha then confirmed what Subhūti had said:
"If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra being preached, is not startled at the beginning, not terrified in the middle, and not afraid at the end."
Regarding unsurpassed enlightenment, they are not startled by its rarity, nor terrified by its profundity, nor daunted by its difficulty to achieve;
thus, they are able to give rise to pure faith in this sutra.
Without further doubt or hesitation, it is certain that one will be able to give rise to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and accomplish immeasurable merit.
This is what is called "firmly grasping the profound meaning. Could there not be such people in the final five hundred years?
They are simply rare. Furthermore, this Dharma-gate is superior to other sūtras; the Buddha has declared it the foremost *pāramitā*.

It is not because it is not the foremost *pāramitā*. Furthermore, it is called the "great cause" because the foremost *pāramitā* can serve as the cause for the Buddhas to cultivate and realize the great essence (*mahātman*). Moreover, it is called "pure" because it is taught in common by immeasurable Buddhas;
its lineage is noble and preeminent, and it is utterly pure. As for those who give precious jewels with it... [no text provided].
When such a multitude of virtues is thus perfected, the merit thereby obtained, when compared to the previous mass of merit, is more than the difference between heaven and earth;
therefore, it is called the most excellent merit among all merits.
"When he practices endurance, although it involves asceticism, because that virtue is immeasurable, it is called a 'superior matter' (*viśeṣa*):
he is able to endure asceticism; since this asceticism is virtuous, his merit is beyond measure. Such is the supreme meaning."
Because he is free from anger and resentment, his state is not called suffering; possessing peaceful bliss and great compassion, his conduct does not result in the fruit of suffering.
Free from the marks of self and anger, there is truly no affliction; together with joy, he possesses loving-kindness and compassion—such is the fruit of ascetic practice.
This explains the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) up to the point where one might give rise to resentment.

That is to say, when those who uphold this sutra practice asceticism, although they share in the same bitter fruits [of suffering], they do not grow weary of these ascetic practices because they possess the nature of endurance (*kṣānti*).
Therefore, it is called "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*). There are two meanings for "the other shore": first, because it is of a virtuous nature (*kuśala-dharma*), by means of all...
The *pāramitās* all have goodness as their essential nature. Second, because those virtues are immeasurable—since no one has ever known their far shore—they are said not to be *pāramitās*.
This ascetic practice is far superior to that sacrifice of the body.
Just as I, at that time, was without the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; I was free from the mark of a self.
Furthermore, when the king repented his transgressions, my mind was free from anger; I was thus separated from the signs of resentment. Because there is no self, there is no one who suffers;
because there is no anger, there is no one who harms others. I saw only shared joy and did not see suffering;
I saw only compassion and did not see hatred. Such are the fruits of ascetic practice: by being in accord with the supreme Dharma, although it is called...

"Enduring patience reaches the other shore; in reality, it is Prajñā that reaches the other shore. How could this be the same as the fruit obtained from giving away one's body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?

(Because the cause for generating the mind does not involve relinquishment, one should therefore seek with firm resolve; this refers to reaching the limit of patience and the skillful means of this mind.)"
It arises from the mind of non-abandonment; through practice and steadfastness, it constitutes the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). One should cultivate that mind capable of learning.
This explanation further recalls how, for five hundred lifetimes in the past, he practiced as a rishi of forbearance.
This leads to the meaning of "not dwelling on signs" when giving. The Buddha is free from signs such as self and person; since five hundred lifetimes ago, he has been practicing.

Because it is firm, it is able to correspond with bodhi. If there is a bodhisattva who does not abandon the marks of self and so forth, then while practicing asceticism, they perceive suffering and distress and consequently wish to relinquish the mind of bodhi. For this reason, one should remain free from all marks;
otherwise, such faults will arise for one who has not yet generated the first thought of bodhi. Therefore, the verse says: "Generating the mind."
Because it is not abandoned, one should therefore seek it with firm resolve. What kind of mind is the cause for the arising of this [bodhicitta]?
One should dispatch oneself to seek it with steadfast diligence. Furthermore, in what respect does the non-abandonment of the bodhicitta serve as the cause that impels further seeking?

The verse says: "For the sake of the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), one practices that mind capable of learning. This refers to the mind of ultimate truth (paramārtha-citta) upon entering the first stage (bhūmi).

Having attained the limit of patience, one practices the non-abiding mind; therefore, the Sūtra speaks of "generating the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta).
Why is this? It is to demonstrate the meaning of generating a mind that does not abide. If the mind were to abide in form (rūpa) and so forth, it would certainly not [attain such a state].
Because one is able to advance toward the fruit of Buddhahood, a bodhisattva should practice giving without abiding anywhere;

this is the skillful means for generating a mind free from abiding and attachment. That is to say, once patience has been attained, even when encountering suffering, one does not abandon the great bodhicitta;
therefore, it is called "practicing that mind capable of learning."

One should know that right practice is the cause for benefiting sentient beings; therefore, one should know how to completely eliminate [clinging to] the entities and characteristics of sentient beings.
One should recognize this as the cause for practicing the benefit of sentient beings, and one should also know the distancing from both sentient beings and their characteristics.
That object refers to the collection of names; the Most Excellent One has removed the notion thereof. The Buddhas do not possess this, because they are endowed with the vision of reality.
Regarding conventional designations and the objects of the aggregates, the Tathāgata is free from those characteristics. The Buddhas do not possess those two, because they perceive the true Dharma.
This explanation is for the benefit of all sentient beings, yet it reaches the meaning of "sentient beings being non-existent.
How is it that one practices for the benefit of sentient beings, and yet further dispels abiding in the act of benefiting sentient beings?
To sever this doubt, the Sūtra says: "For the benefit of sentient beings, one should give in this manner. This refers to the correct practitioner.
This is the cause for benefiting sentient beings, because it does not involve grasping at the characteristics of sentient beings.
What constitutes the affairs of sentient beings? The verse says: "The provisional designation and the aggregates; the Tathāgata is free from those characteristics.

As for those "sentient beings," they are merely established by name and designated as "sentient beings"; this is a provisional designation. Fundamentally, they have no substantial reality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says: "One..."
All marks are, in fact, no-marks. This sufficiently clarifies that there is no self in persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

Furthermore, that upon which sentient beings depend is said to be constituted by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). When one observes these five aggregates with discernment, each lacks a sovereign; in reality, there is nothing that constitutes a sentient being.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says: "All sentient beings are, in fact, no-sentient-beings. This sufficiently clarifies the [selflessness of] phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
There is no self. The Buddhas clearly perceive that those two characteristics are unreal; therefore, those two characteristics do not exist.
Because they see the true mark as being markless, if one sees the ultimate reality, one does not see any person to be delivered, nor does one see any wisdom that delivers.
There is no dwelling or attachment whatsoever; this is the true Dharma of Prajñā.
[It is so. (Although the fruit does not abide in the causal stage, it is the cause for attaining that fruit; because the World-Honored One speaks the truth, one should know there are four kinds).
Although the fruit does not abide in the path, the path can serve as its cause. Because of the truthful words of all Buddhas, that wisdom is of four kinds.
(He establishes the essential teaching of the Hīnayāna and explains the meaning of the Mahāyāna; by virtue of all his prophecies, there is no error whatsoever.
Because his true wisdom, his teaching of the Hīnayāna, his exposition of the Mahāyāna dharma, and all his prophecies are never spoken falsely.
This is the explanation of the fourfold meaning of the Tathāgata’s speech. The Tathāgata’s discourse does not depart from activities such as practicing generosity for the benefit of sentient beings;

this is itself the Path. Although the wondrous fruit of Bodhi does not abide within the discourse of the Path, the discourse of the Path can serve as the cause for Bodhi, because the true language of all Buddhas is able to realize liberation.

This is because his words are indeed [the truth]. His speech consists of four kinds of knowledge. His "True Speech" refers only to the discourse on the true essence and actual wisdom, such as the realm of the *Avataṃsaka*, which is shared with the great Bodhisattvas.

His "Real Speech" refers to such dharmas as the Four Noble Truths and Dependent Origination, which are shared with the followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). His "As-it-is Speech" refers to the discourse on the Mahāyāna and other such dharmas, which are shared with...

It is shared by all bodhisattvas. Regarding "non-different speech": this refers to such utterances as the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth, which only the Tathāgatas can fully exhaust;
these are what are called the "unshared dharmas" (*aveṇika-dharma*). By means of these four, one does not deceive sentient beings.
The Qin translation adds "non-deceptive speech," but this is not something separate from the four; it is not distinct from them.
Speech is fundamentally without deception; that is to say, it is not false. Why then worry that its cause and effect would not correspond?
(Because it does not accord with that [ultimate reality], it is neither real nor false. It is spoken for the sake of those who grasp at words as they are expressed.)

In accordance with that true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*), it is said to be neither unreal nor real. Just as one takes realization upon hearing the sound [of the teaching], such a statement serves as its antidote;

this explains the meaning of this dharma being neither real nor unreal. In conformity with that true knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is said that the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of all dharmas is non-arising.
Since non-arising is the absence of existence, there is no reality. Since there is no arising, how could there be [existence]?
Because it is extinguished, there is no falsehood. Previously, I said that my words are true; now, however, I say they are neither real nor false.
To speak of both at once makes it difficult for the principle to be believed. For this reason, I reply: [I spoke] in response to those who cling to words as they are uttered.
It is like attaining the realization of Bodhi by relying on the teachings of sound, yet then claiming that Bodhi exists within the words themselves. Furthermore...
Hearing the statement that "there is no bodhi within words," one might conclude that bodhi ultimately does not exist at all.

This is because they fail to realize that while words are empty, the Dharma is real. To refute these two types of attachment, it is said that [the Dharma] is "not real," meaning that the taught Dharma cannot itself be the realized Dharma;
this serves as an antidote to the claim that "there is bodhi within words. Furthermore, it is said to be "not false."
This is because the Dharma thus taught accords with that realized Dharma; the realization of the fruit is reality.
Therefore, within the words of the remedy, there is no mention of *bodhi*. Since it is neither real nor unreal, all things should be without abiding.

"At that time and in those places, though they existed, they did not attain the true nature (*tathatā*). Because they lacked wisdom, they dwelt [in phenomena]; because wisdom is non-dwelling, one attains the true.
At that time and in those places, although [the true nature] truly exists, one does not obtain *tathatā*. Due to a lack of wisdom, one abides in dharmas; others, possessing wisdom, attain it.
Ignorance is like darkness; when wisdom is clear, it dispels that darkness. Because the counteragent and its object of elimination, as well as gain and loss, are made manifest:
darkness is like the ignorance of a fool, while clarity is like possessing wisdom. The Abhidharma and its counteragents are likewise for the attainment and cessation of phenomena.
This explains how the mind dwells upon phenomena while practicing generosity, up to the point of perceiving various forms.
"At all times" refers to the past, present, and future; "in all places" refers to the three realms. Sentient beings truly possess the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena.
As for whether this *tathatā* is attained or not attained, it depends on the distinction between the mind dwelling upon phenomena and the mind not dwelling upon them.
If one lacks the wisdom of *prajñā* yet dwells within phenomena (*dharma*), the mind is not pure; it is like being unable to see anything in the darkness.
Although there may be times of liberation and places of *nirvāṇa*, one remains in profound obscurity without awakening, and thus does not attain *tathatā*.
However, if one possesses the wisdom of *prajñā* and does not dwell within phenomena, the mind attains purity; it is like...
One who possesses eyes, when the night has ended and the sun has risen, perceives various forms. At that time, one attains liberation at every moment and enters nirvāṇa in every place;
being transparently luminous and unimpeded, one thus realizes true suchness (*tathatā*). Light and darkness are opposites; this is the nature of "counteracting dharmas" (*pratipakṣa*).
Using wisdom to remedy the lack of wisdom is "antidotal treatment. When light arises, darkness ceases; when wisdom arises, ignorance ceases.

Because one possesses eyes, the capacity for response is revealed; just as when the night has ended, it reveals the exhaustion of the darkness that is to be countered, and just as the light of the sun shines, it reveals the manifestation of the remedial dharma.
Since gain and loss are thus manifest before us, how could we not practice the wisdom of Prajñā?
(Through such correct practice, one obtains such a measure of merit. Regarding those who correctly practice the Dharma, their activity shall now be explained).
In what Dharma does one practice, what measure of merit is obtained, and what further activity is accomplished? Thus is the practice described.
Regarding the text, there are three types: receiving and upholding, reading, and explaining. The meaning is obtained from others and through one's own hearing and reflection.

Names are the three kinds of phenomena; they are received and upheld through extensive explanation and hearing. Cultivation arises from others and internally; by hearing this, one attains the wisdom of cultivation.
(This means: "He ripens himself; others he brings to maturity for the sake of other sentient beings.
This refers to ripening oneself, while the remainder concerns transforming sentient beings.
This explains how one who receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra will achieve immeasurable and boundless merit.
This is the meaning. Regarding the comparison of the excellence of the merit of upholding this sutra: what kind of practice is this? What kind of merit is obtained?
Furthermore, what kind of undertaking is accomplished? To cultivate, uphold, and explain the practice is the correct practice;
to realize the fruit of true suchness is the great merit; and to achieve sovereign power and excellence is the great undertaking.

Practicing in this manner all begins with hearing the sutras. There are three kinds of engagement: receiving and upholding (*udgrahaṇa*), reading and reciting (*vācana-pāṭha*), and expounding (*deśanā*).
If one wishes to receive and uphold the meaning and explain it extensively for others, one must first read and recite the text;

this reading and reciting constitutes the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). Receiving and upholding the meaning constitutes the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*). Having heard the Dharma from another, internally...
Reflecting upon oneself while simultaneously engaging in both [hearing and contemplation] constitutes the attainment of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-jñāna*).

This wisdom of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation is not for the sake of indulging in the play of words; rather, it is for the sake of bringing the innate wisdom of *prajñā* to full maturity within oneself.
With this remaining capacity, one guides and transforms sentient beings, constantly expounding what has been heard extensively for others, so that every person may achieve accomplishment.
The supreme and foremost fruit; this constitutes immeasurable and boundless merit.
*Commentary on the Verses of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Part I (Zongtong, Volume 8);
*Commentary on the Verses of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Part II (Zongtong, Volume 9).
Because of the greatness of the object and the time, the merit is superior among merits;
it is not the domain of others, but is said to depend solely upon a Great Being.
(And it is difficult to hear; the supreme cause increases. If one merely upholds the True Dharma, the locus of reliance becomes a vessel.
And hearing the rare and faithful Dharma, one fulfills the unsurpassed realm; by receiving and upholding the true and wondrous Dharma, one gains merit through honoring the [Buddha] body.

This explains the meaning from the initial offering of bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges during the first part of the day, up to the scattering of various flowers and incense upon that spot.
The act of giving away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is a most vast undertaking;
such is the case for the first part of the day, and so it continues for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. Such is the vastness of the time spent by this person.
One attains merit; indeed, it is the most excellent merit among all merits. Even when compared with such supreme merit, it cannot equal the merit of upholding this sutra.

Thus, this sutra is truly inconceivable and is not something known by others—“others” here referring to those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle, namely the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. This reveals the unique nature of what is obtained.
Merit. Because it is not a common quality shared with the śrāvakas and others, it is taught solely in reliance upon great beings. It is taught for those who have set out in the Mahāyāna;
it cannot be heard by those who have not resolved their minds and entered the bodhisattva stage. It is taught for those who have set out in the Supreme Vehicle (agrayāna);
it cannot be heard by those who have not resolved their minds and entered the Buddha-stage. The Mahāyāna teaching is called the Ultimate Supreme Vehicle. Great.
This vehicle of practice is called the Supreme Vehicle.

If one can generate faith in this Dharma so rarely heard, and can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it for others—this being the most supreme vehicle of the Mahāyāna which is difficult for people to believe—and if one’s faith does not turn back in opposition, then by upholding that Dharma, one is upholding Bodhi; one is able to shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata.
They come toward unsurpassed bodhi and fulfill the unsurpassed dharma-realm.
They are not like those of the two vehicles, who merely delight in inferior dharmas and consider themselves satisfied. Therefore, they are able to receive and uphold such truly wondrous dharmas;
only the Mahāyāna is the most true, and only the Supreme Vehicle is the most wondrous. Using this to explain it for others, all devas...
All people should make offerings to it as they would to a stūpa or temple of the Buddha, scattering various flowers and incense upon that site.
If even the place itself is revered, how could there be anyone who does not revere the person?
Since people revere them, the merit they obtain is likewise inconceivable; how could any superior fortune ever equal it?
(To eliminate all karmic obstructions and swiftly attain the nature of wisdom and supernormal powers).
Furthermore, by remaining far removed from all hindrances, one can again swiftly realize the Dharma.
This explains the meaning of purifying the sinful karma of previous lives until one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, by upholding and expounding this sutra, one not only gains merit but can also eliminate transgressions.

Those karmic obstacles from past lives that would have caused one to fall into the evil realms are eliminated through being treated with contempt and disdain by others in the present life; thus, what was heavy becomes light.
