Once the heavy has been lightened, the light will surely vanish, whereby one remains far removed from all obstacles. This demonstrates the purification of karma.
Regarding the phrase "this is a good thing": it means that when one encounters slighting or humiliation, it reveals that the person being humiliated possesses the nature of merit and virtue;
therefore, it is said that this is a good thing. Furthermore, this does not merely cause one's transgressions to vanish in vain, but can also lead to the realization of the Dharma.
One will be able to swiftly realize the Dharma; this should be seen within the comparison of the merit of making offerings to the Buddha.
The merit of upholding this sutra is thus inconceivably great.
(The excellence of worldly affairs is perfected; the maturation [of its fruit] is most noble. One who practices this Dharma should know that they obtain such karma.)
They accomplish various powers and attain great, wondrous karmic fruits. Such superior deeds as these are known through the practice of the Dharma.
This explains my recollection of the past, extending back through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; even the resulting karmic retribution is inconceivable.
Before encountering Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the Buddha made offerings to many Buddhas throughout countless kalpas. Only then...
One can attain Buddhahood. By upholding this sutra, one will swiftly realize Bodhi.

Compared to the merit of making offerings to all Buddhas, this [merit] is more than ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or a billion times greater; it even exceeds what can be reached by calculation or analogy.
No such various powers can equal it. The resulting retribution is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable. This is precisely...
It is the perfection of all wondrous worldly matters and possesses the most exalted retribution;
this is because it encompasses all perfections belonging to the World-Protectors, Śakra, the Brahmins, and others. Because it is immeasurable and boundless, it is called "Great."
This is precisely the nature of multiplicity. Because it is inconceivable, it is called "wondrous. This is precisely the nature of supremacy.
Since it cannot be fathomed by ordinary minds, one attains the great and wondrous fruit.

Thus, the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless, most supreme activities all arises from the practice of the True Dharma; thereby, one is able to abide securely in such manifold virtues. Therefore—
Those who uphold this sutra practice according to the three methods of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation;

only then can they give rise to the wondrous wisdom of non-abiding and realize the unsurpassed, sublime fruit. One should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic retribution is likewise inconceivable;
it is known only by the practitioner themselves.
"When one practices by means of one's own person, taking oneself to be a bodhisattva, this is called a mental obstruction; it contradicts the mind that does not dwell.
When practicing within the inner mind, maintaining the notion "I am a bodhisattva," this constitutes an obstruction to the mind and contradicts the path of non-abiding.

What does this explanation mean by "how one should abide"? It refers to the meaning of the statement that, in reality, there is no dharma whatsoever that gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for the previous phrase, "how one should abide," it intends that one should subdue [the mind] and dwell in peace.
How should this abide? It is because one suspects that it must be subdued in order to abide. This is because there is still a self existing.
If, while practicing within the mind, one thinks there is a dharma or a self, one immediately becomes attached to the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
This is an obstruction to wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It can obstruct the mind and is truly contrary to the Way of Non-abiding; thus, it cannot be called [the Way].
As for being a bodhisattva, if one discusses the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is originally no arising;
in reality, there is no dharma whatsoever that can give rise to the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

If even the very first moment of giving rise to the thought of enlightenment does not exist, how could there be a "self" that dwells within it and subdues [the mind]? Since there is simply no self, there is nothing to dwell upon. This is the internal...
The mind practices conduct that is in accord with reality; a bodhisattva should abide in this manner.
(Because the prediction for a later time has been bestowed, the practice under Dīpaṃkara was not superior. Enlightenment and those practices are identical; it is not truly produced by causes.)
The prophecy was given for a future time; however, the practice of Dīpaṃkara was not superior. That practice is equal to awakening; it does not have the characteristic of being truly conditioned.

(Because it lacks those [conditioned] characteristics as its characteristic, it reveals that it is not false. Since these dharmas are the Buddha-dharmas, none of them possess the characteristics of the conditioned.)
That is precisely the characteristic of non-characteristic. Because it is taught as being non-deceptive, this dharma is the dharma of all Buddhas; it is the self-nature characteristic of all things.
This explains that when the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he attained this state and was therefore named "One Who Embodies the Meaning of All Dharmas.
Formerly, Dīpaṃkara bestowed a prophecy upon Śākyamuni that he would later become a Buddha. At the time of Dīpaṃkara, there was no superior practice.
Because one can realize awakening at that place, one receives the prediction [of enlightenment].
If awakening were non-existent, the Buddha would also be non-existent. To sever this doubt, it is said that "the Tathāgata" is "suchness" (tathatā).
Although not a single dharma can be apprehended, it is not that the Tathāgata does not exist; therefore, the Tathāgata is the true nature, suchness. That is to say, there is no...
Perversion is called the true nature (*dharmatā*), meaning it is without change; this is called *tathatā*.
If someone were to say that the Tathāgata attains unsurpassed enlightenment—that the practice of the bodhisattva path is substantially existent—this would be false and delusory.
If one says that there is actually an attainment of unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*), this too is false.
A verse states: "Enlightenment is equal to those practices," and so forth. The Dharma is the Dharma of enlightenment, and the Buddha is enlightenment; how could there be an attainment?
If there is neither practice nor attainment, does it mean that the Tathāgata ultimately has nothing attained? To sever this doubt, he speaks as follows:
The Dharma of enlightenment that is attained is neither real nor unreal. As for what is called "not real," the verse states:
"Because it does not possess the characteristics of conditioned phenomena. Conditioned phenomena refer to such things as the five aggregates (*skandhas*), which are truly produced by causes.

Since that Dharma of enlightenment lacks the characteristics of form and so forth, the absence of such characteristics as form constitutes its intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*); that itself is enlightenment.
Because it characterizes the sign. The verse says: "The absence of that sign is itself the sign. It further says: "That very thing is the sign of non-sign.
Because it is taught as being non-false, it is called "non-illusory. Being neither real nor illusory, attainment is itself non-attainment; yet this is the dharma of non-attainment.
This does not mean that one merely realizes the principle of emptiness while failing to encompass all things. The Buddha has taught all things.
All dharmas take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their essence. Since True Suchness is realized only by the Buddha, it is said that they are all "Buddha-dharmas.

However, all these dharmas—such as form and sound—are originally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they cannot maintain their own substantiality and are therefore not "all dharmas" in the ultimate sense.
Because they are not [ultimately] all dharmas, but are simply True Suchness, they are called "all dharmas."
This "all" is the all of True Suchness (tathatā). These "dharmas" are the self-nature and characteristics of True Suchness itself.
Therefore, it is said: "These dharmas are the dharmas of all Buddhas; they are the self-nature and characteristics of all."
(That is to say, one should understand that the Dharmakāya Buddha is illustrated by the metaphor of a man; for his unobstructed and perfectly complete body is of a pervasive nature.
Based upon that Dharmakāya Buddha, the metaphor of the "great body" is taught; this body is free from all obstructions and pervades all objects.
Furthermore, because it has attained the greatness of essence, it is also called the "Great Body. It is not that a body exists as a body; rather, it is said that what is made is a non-body.
Because of its merits and its great essence, it is therefore called the Great Body. That which is a non-body is itself the body; for this reason, it is called a non-body.
This explanation is like the analogy of a human body being tall and large; it culminates in the meaning of what is called the "Great Body.
In the preceding text, the Buddha said that what is not a body is called the Great Body; this merely uses "non-body" to manifest the Dharma-body, referring to the empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Here, the Tathāgata says that a human body being tall and large is precisely what is not a great body, and is therefore called the Great Body. This includes—
The phrase "the human body is large" manifests the *dharmakāya*. This refers to the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
The Buddha-dharma pervades all places; that is, *tathatā* (suchness) pervades all places. This *tathatā-dharmakāya* is the greatest, just as the human body is large.
It is in accordance with the *dharmakāya* that it is called a "large body," yet this is not separate from the human body when one speaks of a large body.
Furthermore, the Dharma-body cannot exist apart from all things while manifesting its own greatness;

therefore, it is able to remain far removed from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), thereby being fully endowed with the Dharma-body. First, it pervades all places; such is the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because among all phenomena there is no distinct nature, secondly, its merit is great: the merit of its cultivation is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable;
it is able to correspond with the Great Essence, which is precisely the realization of the Great Essence.
For this reason, it is called the "Great Body. Subhūti clearly understood this meaning;
therefore, he said that when the Tathāgata speaks of the Dharma-body as pervading all places, it is like a human body being large and tall.
However, although the Dharma-body pervades all places, because it is not a conditioned (saṃskṛta) body, it is not a "Great Body. This very non-Greatness...
The body is called the "wondrous great body," for it is the very nature of *tathatā* (suchness). This body is precisely no-body;
no-body is precisely the body. Therefore, when it is said to be "no-body," this is spoken in reliance upon that *dharmakāya*.
The *dharmakāya* is not separate from all things, and all things are not separate from the *dharmakāya*. How could this possibly refer merely to a partial emptiness or a non-body?
(Not understanding the dharma-realm, yet conceiving the intention to deliver sentient beings and to purify the buddha-field—this is called deception and falsehood.
Failing to penetrate the true dharma-realm, one gives rise to the intention to save sentient beings and to purify the land; the very arising of such a mind is an inversion.
(Regarding bodhisattvas and sentient beings: all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Although understanding this is not [yet] noble, it should be known as "noble wisdom.
Sentient beings and bodhisattvas know that all phenomena are selfless; this is the conviction of their own non-noble wisdom, as well as the wisdom of the noble ones.
This explanation of the bodhisattva is likewise so. To reach ultimate reality is the true meaning of "bodhisattva. It was stated above that not a single dharma can be apprehended;
yet all dharmas are themselves the Buddha-dharma. This is the true dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which is realized only by the Tathāgata.

It is not only the Tathāgata who is thus; the Bodhisattva is likewise so. The true realm (*dharmadhātu*) is equal and devoid of such characteristics as self, person, sentient being, or life-span. In reality, there is no dharma that can be called a "Bodhisattva.

If one does not penetrate this, yet gives rise to thoughts and mental activities, desiring to save sentient beings or to adorn Buddha-lands, then the subject-object mind has not been forgotten. In that case—
This is perversion. One who is subject to perversion is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), not a bodhisattva.
If one thoroughly penetrates the dharma of selflessness, there are two kinds of such dharmas: first, those belonging to sentient beings; second, those belonging to bodhisattvas.
If one possesses innate wisdom and can have faith—whether it be mundane wisdom or supramundane wisdom—one will believe and understand.

All phenomena are without intrinsic nature. All phenomena are without intrinsic nature. Not only are they free from the self of persons (*pudgala-ātman*), but they are also free from the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*).
Although these individuals are not yet noble ones (*ārya*), they already possess noble wisdom; therefore, it is said that they are indeed Bodhisattvas.
One is a Bodhisattva according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the other is a Bodhisattva according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); hence, the words "this is truly" are repeated.
A bodhisattva is indeed a bodhisattva. How does he differ from the Tathāgata’s true dharma-realm?
(Although he does not perceive all phenomena, this is not because he lacks eyes; the Buddha is able to possess five kinds [of vision], for objects are illusory.)

Although they do not perceive any phenomena, it is not that they lack the eye that comprehends objects. Because the five kinds of reality of the Buddhas see those inversions [as such], the various mental streams flow on;
because they are devoid of the foundations of mindfulness, they dwell nowhere yet constantly revolve, and are therefore said to be false.
Various inverted consciousnesses arise because they are separated from true mindfulness and do not abide in that true wisdom; therefore, they are called "inverted.
This explains the meaning of the five eyes. Although Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize that not a single dharma can be apprehended, does it mean they see nothing at all?
They clearly illuminate the objects before them through five kinds of true wisdom-eyes. To see is to know; to know is [to realize].
This is precisely what is seen. Therefore, one is able to know the various kinds of minds of sentient beings.
Because those various minds abide in falsehood and do not abide in the true wisdom of *tathatā*, they are called "non-minds.

Because they are far removed from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they lack any sustained grasping and revolve perpetually following the current; thus, they are named "distracted and scattered minds. This is the flow.
The distracted mind is precisely inversion. How is this inversion made clear? Because in the past, present, and future, no mind can be apprehended.

Thus, by examining the present through the past and the future, all various discriminations are seen to be empty and false, ultimately returning to non-existence. Since no nature of the three periods of time can be apprehended, it is so named.

It is said that this is a reversal of the truth. The Tathāgata has realized the true mind, whereas the various deluded minds of sentient beings are all merely partial phenomena manifested within that true mind. How could there be anything he does not fully know and fully see?
(One should know that this is the sustenance of wisdom; thus, merit is not in vain. To manifest these causes of merit, the parable is stated again.
The root of the Buddha’s wisdom is non-perverted merit. Because it possesses the characteristics of such merit, the parable is explained once more.
This explanation clarifies the meaning that even if someone were to fill the three-thousandfold world system [with offerings], the merit they would obtain would not be great.
That which dwells upon signs when practicing giving lacks the root of wisdom and thus becomes a cause for outflows (*āsrava*).
Although it possesses the nature of merit, it is a perverted virtue; therefore, it is not sufficient to be considered much. If one practices giving without dwelling upon signs...
This giving is sustained by the wisdom of perfect enlightenment and constitutes the cause for the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Although it lacks the aggregates of merit-taking (*upādāna-skandha*), its merit is truly inconceivable. It cannot be discussed by analogy with the inverted consciousnesses of those sentient beings;

even if one were to employ repeated metaphors, their meaning would remain somewhat different. Previously, Subhūti compared the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) with the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Therefore, because worldly merit is so abundant, it does not equal its absence. This Buddha takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as identical to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
it is precisely because of the absence of merit that he speaks of its abundance. The Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that the merit obtained is immeasurable;
how could this be compared to those various deluded minds which are unobtainable?
(It should be understood that in the true *dharmakāya*, there is no perfection of secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), nor is it possessed of primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);

it is not of the nature of a body. The ultimate essence of the *dharmakāya* is not that body of marks and signs, because it is not accomplished by means of marks, and it is not that [conventional] *dharmakāya*.
(There is no distinction within the dharmakāya; it is not that there are no two Tathāgatas. The phrase is repeated to indicate the possession of marks, because both entities are non-existent.
Not apart from the dharmakāya, those two are not non-Buddhas; therefore, "accomplishment" is stated again. Furthermore, there is neither duality nor existence.
Can one see the Buddha by means of this so-called "body of complete form"? This refers to the meaning of being "endowed with all marks.
The essence of the Dharma-body Tathāgata is ultimately empty and quiescent;
it is not that body characterized by the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. For the essence of the Dharma-body cannot be accomplished through conditioned marks.
Therefore, the body endowed with the marks and signs is not that Dharma-body. Thus, the Sūtra says: "One should not see [the Buddha] by means of the body complete in form;
one should not see [him] by means of the body complete in all marks.

Nevertheless, these two types—the marks and signs—are not non-Buddha, because these two are not separate from the Dharma-body; the marks and signs are themselves the Dharma-body. Therefore, it is stated again.
It is accomplished. Thus, the Sūtra says: "This is called the fulfillment of the form-body; this is called the fulfillment of all marks.
According to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one should not perceive the Dharma-body through physical characteristics; therefore, it is said to be "not a body.

This explains that the Buddha’s attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is what is meant by the term "the meaning of wholesome dharmas.

It is attained; it is the very locus of bodhi. This unsurpassed bodhi is the nature of the dharmadhātu. The dharmadhātu is equal:

Cultivation is attained through deliberate practice. There must be the unsurpassed skillful means;
there is no wholesome dharma that is not directly realized, and no wholesome dharma that is not perfectly awakened to.

Furthermore, one remains far removed from all outflow-tainted dharmas pertaining to self, person, sentient being, or life-span, thereby realizing the fruit of the untainted. The untainted is itself the wholesome.

However, that which is called "wholesome dharma" by the Tathāgata is said to be "not a dharma. Because wholesome dharmas possess a substantial nature, they serve as the means for realizing the principle of non-apprehension;

since their nature is not [identical to] that [principle], they are "not pure. Nevertheless, because those [dharmas] are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they may be called "not wholesome"; yet those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) are definitively wholesome.

Although it is said that the indeterminate dharmas have no [discernible] cause, this very teaching reveals their cause. Therefore, the single Jewel of the Dharma surpasses immeasurable worldly treasures.
(Even among all categories of calculation and estimation, there is a difference in their causes; when one investigates the world, no analogy can reach it.)
The power of its number is incomparably supreme; its cause is likewise incomparable. No worldly phenomena can serve as a metaphor for it.
This explanation refers to the meaning of reaching that which cannot be reached, even within a trichiliocosm.

First, they are unequal in strength, like the difference between the powerful and the weak. Second, they are unequal in stature, like the difference between a noble person and a commoner.

(Because the dharma-realm is equal, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings; he gathers with all names, yet remains not outside the dharma-realm).
In the equal and true Dharma-realm, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings. Because names are common to those aggregates, they do not depart from the Dharma-realm.
(If one gives rise to attachment to phenomena, it is the same fault as attachment to a self. To insistently grasp at the liberation of sentient beings is a false attachment born of non-attachment.)
To grasp at me as one who has crossed over is an error; to grasp at those dharmas is correct, because it is for the sake of delivering sentient beings. One should not grasp at them as being thus.
This interpretation is intended so that you do not think that the Tathāgata has such a thought; this is what is meant by the term "ordinary person. As the Sūtra says:
"In truth, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata has delivered. This refers to the midst of the single, true Dharma-realm of equality.
The Buddha is this dharma-realm; sentient beings are this dharma-realm. How could there be a dharma-realm that transcends the dharma-realm?

Therefore, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings. As for the name "sentient beings," it has no name. Sentient beings are constituted by depending upon the five aggregates (*skandhas*), yet the aggregates have no self-nature as aggregates.

For one who wishes to cause sentient beings to definitely attain liberation, such signs must not be grasped. However, although the Tathāgata...

Desiring to lead all sentient beings to the same realization of non-self, and for the purpose of delivering sentient beings, I have spoken of a self. Its...
The grasping at a self can be known; yet those ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) who are bound by the notion of "mine," the Tathāgata says are not actually ordinary beings.
Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), no ordinary being can be found at all; they are merely called "ordinary beings" according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Since there is no ordinary being, where could there be a self? This name "ordinary being" does not exist apart from the dharma-dhātu. Ordinary...

The Tathāgata cannot be known by means of comparison with the marks of the physical body. All Buddhas possess only the Dharma-body; a Cakravartin king is not a Buddha.

(Although he possesses the fruits of retribution consisting of the complete marks and perfect merit, he is not permitted [to attain Buddhahood]; yet it is possible for him to attract the Dharma-body through the distinct nature of his skillful means.)
It is not the fruit of marks and signs; rather, by relying on the accomplishment of merit and virtue, one attains the true Dharma-body.

Because its manifestations through skillful means differ from these [marks], those who merely see forms and hear sounds do not know the Buddha. This is because this true Suchness-Dharma-body is not an object of consciousness.

The body. Because the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is not an object of cognition, it cannot be understood [by consciousness]. As the verse says: "Because the *dharmakāya* of true suchness (*tathatā*) is not an objective sphere of consciousness.

Since full understanding cannot be attained, how could the Dharma-body be perceived through comparison? Thus, the Sūtra says: 'One should [perceive it] by means of its various marks...'"
One does not perceive the Tathāgata through signs; the meaning is complete herein:
(one’s merit shall not be lost, the retribution shall not be severed, and the attainment of patience shall likewise not be interrupted, because one has acquired the stainless state).

(To further discuss the causes of merit, this analogy is presented: because that merit has no [further] retribution, one correctly takes what is to be taken and does not take beyond that.)
To demonstrate the marks of supreme merit, this parable is therefore spoken. This merit is without retribution; thus one experiences it without grasping.
This explains that if you should think in such a way, it leads to this: therefore, the meaning of "not receiving merit" is taught. The Tathāgata truly cannot be seen by means of marks.
If one clings to the destruction of marks as being correct, claiming that it is not necessary to be complete in the characteristics of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa).
To realize awakening through [merely] observing signs is to lose both the cultivation of the causes of merit and the attainment of the superior fruit of fruition;
this is the biased view of emptiness held by the two vehicles. A bodhisattva who has resolved their mind must necessarily rely on the simultaneous integration of wisdom and compassion.
I do not speak of the characteristic of the annihilation of all phenomena. Adornment through wisdom is the cause of merit;
the accomplishment of blessings is the supreme retribution. Without losing one's merit, one realizes Bodhi;

If one knows that all phenomena are without self and thereby achieves patience, this is giving without dwelling upon signs.

One realizes the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness, and the merit thus obtained is pure and stainless, beyond the reach of worldly merit. By means of this supreme patience, [one attains this state].
One attains the fruit of stainlessness; this is the mark of supreme merit. Therefore, it is said that this surpasses the merit previously attained by the bodhisattva.
How is it known that it is superior? Because the bodhisattva is entirely without self; although they possess merit, they do not receive its retribution.
The reason they do not receive it is that they do not perceive any merit to which they might become attached. If they were to grasp...
If one clings to merit, one remains within birth and death; though one may obtain the retribution of merit, it is merely that of a wheel-turning monarch and cannot be called Buddhahood.
Only by not grasping does one realize non-arising. Since the cause is untainted (*anāsrava*), the fruit is also untainted.
Although one does not lose one's merits or those superior retributions, one truly does not undergo retribution, because there is no longer any tainted retribution. Thus it is grasped.
This is called "correct grasping," and is therefore termed the "stainless fruit. This is why it is superior:

(while that merit invites transformational fruits and performs deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, those activities proceed spontaneously, and upon attaining Buddhahood, one manifests in all directions).
This is the retribution for merit; yet, in order to transform all sentient beings, such karma occurs spontaneously.
The Buddhas appear throughout the ten directions (though coming and going are merely manifestations, while Perfect Enlightenment is eternally unmoving).
The transformation-body Buddhas of the past and future—the Tathāgata is eternally unmoving.
This explains that if someone says [the Buddha] "comes," it is the meaning of the term *tathāgata*. As stated above, he does not accept merit.

Thus, the Buddhas appear throughout the ten directions like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers; this is simply natural and effortless.
There is indeed this activity, yet it is not the case that there is any real coming or going within it. Coming and going refers only to the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha.
A transformation body is like a magical illusion; fundamentally, it is not truly real. As for the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata, he is pure and all-pervasive;
he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. He is eternally unmoving—how could he possess the characteristics of coming and going, sitting or lying down?
Yes. If one can understand the meaning of the Tathāgata as taught by the Buddha, then even this manifested Buddha does not exist;
how much less could there be any matter of receiving blessings?
(One should know that within the sphere of the dharma-realm, it is neither one nor different. The analogy of reducing atoms to ink illustrates the dharma-realm.
Thus, within the sphere of the dharma-realm, it is neither one nor different. The world being reduced to atoms—this analogy demonstrates that meaning.

(This treatise describes the process of making ink. It is for the sake of exhausting the afflictions that act as obstacles. Its nature is neither an accumulation nor a collection; it reveals a nature that is not unitary.
By crushing fine dust into powder, the exhaustion of afflictions is demonstrated. Because it is not a collection, it is a collection; it is not merely a single metaphor.
Regarding that nature of total aggregation, it is clarified as not being a distinct nature; yet the ignorant fail to understand this and merely follow conventional speech, falsely clinging to it.
That which is the locus of aggregation is not [the object itself], nor is it a metaphor for differentiation; ordinary people grasp at it erroneously, following only the sounds [of words].
This commentary explains that the trichiliocosm is ground into atoms; this reaches the point of the meaning of being attached to those matters.
That is to say, while the aforementioned transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) has coming and going, the dharma-body (dharmakāya) is eternally unmoving.

Between these two, there is in reality no characteristic of either identity or difference; therefore, the Buddha clarifies this by means of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Whether coming or going, sitting or reclining, it does not depart from the dharma-body.
For example, just as minute particles are not separate from the world, yet they cannot be said to be one, nor can they be said to be different;
so too, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not abide in a single location within the *dharmadhātu* of true suchness (*tathatā*), nor do they abide in separate locations.
Why clarify that they are neither one nor different? It is because that world is shattered into minute particles; this is used as a metaphor.
This refers to the meaning of the Dharma-body manifesting through coming, going, sitting, and reclining.
To reduce fine dust into powder and thereby form a single world of empty space is used as a metaphor for the exhaustion of afflictions and the realization of the signless Dharma-body.
That great empty space does not constitute a world by means of the accumulation of fine dust; rather, it is this [space]...
Dust is inherently without self-nature; it is not that something existent combines to form the world—this cannot be used as a metaphor for unity.
Furthermore, at the place where subtle particles aggregate, it is not that the world can produce those particles;
the world is fundamentally without self-nature, and it is not that something existent disperses to form subtle particles—this cannot be used as a metaphor for difference.
This is a metaphor. The Dharma-body is itself the transformation-body; it does not abide in a single location. The transformation-body is itself the Dharma-body;
it does not abide in a different location. Who could perceive any matter of division or union?

It is only because ordinary beings do not realize that the world is fundamentally empty that they believe there truly exists a phenomenon of union. This is to perceive existence within that which has no existence. This...

(One abandons both self and dharmas; it is not because of the non-attainment of awakening. Therefore, seeing non-existence is the false attachment to a non-existent object.

"Because this is a subtle obstacle, it is abandoned through such knowledge; by attaining two kinds of wisdom and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is then removed.
"This is a subtle obstacle; by seeing *tathatā* (suchness), one becomes free from it. Through the two wisdoms and samādhi, one thus attains liberation."
This commentary explains that if someone says, "The Buddha taught the view of self," this refers to the meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Although not a single dharma can be apprehended on the path to unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*), one must possess the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) in order to realize and enter it.
Therefore, it is said that the path cannot be attained without these two wisdoms; one must remain far removed from the mark of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*).
There are four kinds. Only after one has realized these four characteristics of phenomena can one attain realization.
If one perceives a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, one does not see bodhi.

One who does not know that these four marks are fundamentally not substantially existent—since they lack reality, they are non-entities—speaks of the view of self as a false view. If one perceives the existence of dharmas...
As for "characteristics," one does not even perceive bodhi. Therefore, those who have resolved to attain bodhi should know, see, and believe in this way:
they should not give rise to the notion of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Because by perceiving the characteristics of dharmas, one does not perceive characteristics;

it is just as when one perceives a self (*ātman*), one does not [truly] perceive it. Why are these two types of views called "non-perception"? This is because they are subtle obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that coexist [with wisdom].

Grasping at a self of persons and grasping at phenomena as inherently existent—these are called the subtle obstacles. Upon seeing *tathatā* (suchness), one immediately becomes free from these obstacles.

How is it that one comes to see *tathatā*? It is by knowing thus, seeing thus, and resolving with faith thus, that one attains the wisdom of the emptiness of persons and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena; these are called the two wisdoms. Know that these arise based on meditative concentration.
Vision arises based on wisdom; faith and understanding arise based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom, and mental stability. This is called *samādhi*.
When one possesses these two types of knowledge and this *samādhi*, one is detached from phenomena within phenomena and detached from marks within marks.
Not giving rise to the conceptualization of phenomena, one abides nowhere and is thus able to subdue the mind. What two obstacles could there possibly be?
The emanation body of Chen Fuming possesses inexhaustible merit; when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do not say that this body is an emanation.
The emanation bodies manifested by the Buddhas possess inexhaustible merit; when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do not say, "This is an emanation body."
(Because he does not speak for himself, it is his true teaching).

This explains the meaning of "if there is someone who fills the immeasurable" up to "the state of immovable suchness. Although the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body)...

One who might bestow the seven treasures upon immeasurable and incalculable worlds would obtain inexhaustible merit;
yet, one who gives rise to the bodhicitta and upholds and expounds this sutra acts as a substitute for the transformation Buddhas to preach the Dharma, and the merit obtained thereby is superior.
That immeasurable giving is not without inexhaustible merit. How is it that this exposition surpasses it?
It is because when the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they always act in accordance with reality;

they do not grasp at signs, nor do they say, "I am a transformation body," nor do they maintain the characteristics of a speaker or something spoken. Now, this expositor is like that True Suchness (tathatā), and does not grasp [at signs].
Regarding characteristics, there is likewise neither the characteristic of a speaker nor the characteristic of that which is spoken.
Since it is not for the sake of others that one proclaims and reveals [it], it is therefore called "proclaiming and revealing for others.

(The realization of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is neither created nor distinct [from it]. This collection of creations consists of nine [aspects], because they are observed through correct wisdom.)
The nirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas is neither conditioned nor separate from it, because of the correct contemplation of the nine types of conditioned phenomena by means of sublime wisdom:
(the seeing, the appearance, and the consciousness; the dwelling place, the body, and the objects of enjoyment; as well as the past, the present, and the future, which are minutely examined).
One perceives the marks, consciousness, the vessel-world, the body, and the objects of enjoyment; one likewise contemplates past and present phenomena, as well as those of the future world.
(By observing these marks, through the enjoyment and the flux of conditioned things, one attains stainless mastery over all conditioned phenomena.)
One contemplates characteristics and enjoyments, and contemplates the three periods of time. Within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), one attains stainless mastery.
Why is this explained? It is because one should understand the meaning as follows:
since the Proclaimer is already suchness (*tathatā*) and immovable, for what reason does the Tathāgata enter *nirvāṇa*? Nevertheless, the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata does not abide in existence.

It is conditioned, yet it is not separate from the conditioned. Just as with the nine kinds of conditioned phenomena, when one contemplates them with the sublime wisdom of *prajñā*, permanence is itself impermanence, and impermanence is itself permanence. Therefore, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) does not obstruct the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and the dharma-body does not obstruct nirvāṇa.
As for what are called the "nine kinds," they are like a star, a visual impairment, a lamp, an illusion, dew, and a bubble.

namely, that all karma is like an illusion; that [the world] is seen like stars, vanishing once wisdom arises; that characteristics are like cataracts, produced by diseased eyes;
that consciousness is like a lamp, continuing in a succession of moments; that the vessel-world is like a magical creation, lacking a single real essence; and that the body...
Like dew, it abides but for a moment; that is, its enjoyment is like a bubble, which disperses as soon as it forms.
The past is like a dream, arising only from memory. The present is like lightning, not remaining for even a single kṣaṇa. The future is like a cloud.

Containing moisture, it becomes rain; this is fully explained as before. The foolish and erroneous interpretation [takes this] to refer to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), as well as the subtle matters of the eight consciousnesses.
That which is subsumed under the image-part refers to the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), the internal faculties and bodies, and the resources for enjoyment;
these are certainly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). That which is subsumed under the seeing-part refers to past actions.

The causal conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma, as well as all dharmas currently functioning, are stored within the field of the eight consciousnesses. Furthermore, they serve as the basis for various experiences in future lives;
these too are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). When observing their characteristics and their experiential enjoyment, they extend horizontally throughout the ten directions.
When observing the events of the three periods of time, they penetrate vertically through the three temporal limits. One should be able to observe them with sublime wisdom in this manner.

Dreams, illusions, and the like, arise and perish in an instant; they have never existed from the beginning. This is attaining purity and stainlessness within conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Since there is neither arising nor ceasing, it is suchness (*tathatā*), immovable. This is [attaining purity] within conditioned phenomena.
This is the attainment of great mastery. It is the Dharmakāya of True Suchness (Tathatā).

Fundamentally, it is not conditioned (saṃskṛta), yet it is also not separate from the conditioned. Because it is not conditioned, it has never come; because it is not separate from the conditioned, it has never gone.
Thus, the Tathāgata is like that which fundamentally has no coming or going. As for the teaching of the Dharma, it is like suchness itself, which is inherently...
It is immovable; it speaks of dust and speaks of lands, fundamentally without interruption. Why, then, be so attached to the appearance of entering nirvana?
One who contemplates in this manner possesses right contemplation. Were it not for the wondrous wisdom of prajñā, who could do such a thing?

The rare dhāraṇī-dharma of all Buddhas, its profound phrases and meanings are immeasurable;
Having received the resolution from the Honored One, the meaning is widely expounded, so that one may obtain merit and swiftly bring about purification.
Having heard from the Venerable One and having heard his extensive exposition, I dedicate this merit to all living beings.
Zeng Fengyi remarked: "This verse was transmitted by Maitreya Bodhisattva to Asaṅga, and Asaṅga transmitted it to Vasubandhu.
Among its subtle phrasing and profound meanings, it is not easy to comprehend; we rely upon Asaṅga and Vasubandhu [for their elucidation]."
Each [of these] has its own commentary (*śāstra*), and each commentary is concise yet profound. There are over several dozen sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*);

among them, only Zixuan of Changshui’s *Kandingji* (Record of Collated Determination) is considered precise and appropriate. However, it still does not fully include the verses of Maitreya cited therein.

Recently, I obtained a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with its verses carved by the lay practitioner He Dehui of Luling; furthermore, this version also does not record the transmission from Maitreya.
Regarding these causes and conditions, the reader may find it difficult to understand this verse as it has not been analyzed.

I, Yi, being of dull wit, have erroneously composed the *Vajra-yuan-tong* (Penetration of the Vajra Source) and have here recorded this verse again with a new commentary, requesting correction from virtuous spiritual friends throughout the four quarters.
